title: Serving-as-Moat-Narrative One-pager
body:
TL;DR:
Redwood’s strategic narrative: we sell the operational advantage of serving LLMs, not just access to models. The core claim is that superior serving — predictable latency, repeatable unit costs, and out-of-the-box operational controls — is the defensible moat that turns model capability into reliable product value.

Mission line (single sentence):
Make LLM inference an owned, measurable capability for engineering teams — fast to ship, cheap to run, and safe to operate.

Why this matters now: short context
- The market is saturated with model access — what differentiates production apps is how models are served at scale.
- Early experiments focus on capability; production success is about consistent economics and operational risk.
- Customers are moving from “trying models” to “running models in product” and they need predictable costs and reliability guarantees.

Core thesis (3-proposition):
1) Serving is the new moat: Companies win by operationalizing inference — reducing token cost, stabilizing latency, and embedding graceful degradation policies.
2) One runtime across deployment modes: A single control plane that maps to hosted, reserved, and private infrastructure removes engineering divergence and accelerates rollout.
3) Developer-first means production-ready: developer experience must include observability, rollback/rollout workflows, and cost controls, not just a simple SDK.

Key positioning pillars (short bullets with quick evidence hooks):
- Predictable unit economics — Suggest customers can see 2x–4x lower token cost with batching, caching, and quantization profiles; show one-sentence case study later.
- Operational continuity — Built-in fallbacks (model variants, region failover) and SLAs designed for user-facing apps.
- Unified developer surface — Same API, same SDKs, same telemetry whether hosted or in-customer VPC.
- Quality-first automation — Eval-driven regression alerts and prompt sets that prevent rollouts from silently degrading UX.

Persona-focused one-liners (for decks / sales scripts):
- Software engineer / ML engineer: “Ship the feature without rebuilding a serving stack — keep latency predictable while trimming token cost.”
- Platform/Infra lead: “Standardize inference across teams: one runtime, policy-driven routing, and per-route cost controls.”
- Procurement/Legal: “Choose a supplier that gives predictable spend, auditable ops, and private deployment options for regulated data.”

Proof points / evidence to collect (R&D + GTM):
- Benchmarks: median p95 latency across 512-token workloads on standard configs, and comparisons to popular managed endpoints.
- Economics: anonymized customer example showing % cost reduction from caching + batching + int8 quantization.
- Reliability: story of automated rollback during a model regression and how traffic was automatically routed to a fallback variant.

Competitive framing (how to talk about peers):
- Not just model catalogs: competitors sell models or simple endpoints — our hammer is serving behavior and system-level guarantees.
- Not just infra: pure infra vendors leave teams to stitch telemetry, rollout, and fallbacks — we package the policy layer + telemetry + runtime.
- Not just cost-cut tools: some vendors focus on token savings or quantization only; Redwood couples savings with SLO-safe controls so cost optimizations don’t break UX.

Common sales objections + rebuttals (short):
- "We can self-host and save money" → Rebuttal: self-hosting hides costs in engineering time and ops fragility; our Dedicated/Private options let you control spend without building the orchestration and safety layer.
- "We only need model access, not a platform" → Rebuttal: model access is necessary but not sufficient for production; we convert model output into product outcomes by guaranteeing latency, fallback, and observability.
- "Lock-in concerns" → Rebuttal: same API across hosted, dedicated, and private means customers can migrate deployment modes with minimal code change; we support exportable metrics, model version pinning, and open model variants.

Suggested one-line hero messaging options (pick 1–2 for A/B):
- "Turn model capability into product certainty."
- "Predictable inference: cost, latency, and reliability you can measure."

Metrics we’ll use to prove the narrative (GTM + Product):
- Time-to-first-successful-rollout (developer experience metric).
- Cost per 1k useful tokens vs. top managed alternatives.
- % of customer routes using automated fallback or canary in first 90 days.
- Regression-detection to rollback time (mean minutes).

Next steps (for this doc):
1) Align with product on two concrete benchmark narratives to publish: latency/cost and rollback story. (Owners: Eng serving + Product)
2) Draft a 1-pager customer case that highlights a measurable cost and reliability win (GTM + CS).
3) Convert hero lines into A/B testable homepage banners and a short explainer video script (Marketing).
4) Map objections into one-pagers for sales playbooks (Sales Enablement).

Collateral to produce quickly:
- One-page benchmark sheet (numbers + config)
- 90-second demo script (showing failover and cost dashboard)
- Sales FAQ doc with competitor comparisons and short rebuttal phrases

Notes / open questions (working items):
- Which internal benchmark rig will we standardize on for public claims? (INF-bench-choices: 256 vs 512 token profiles)
- Can SRE provide anonymized rollback incident for a public case study?
- What are guardrails on quantization claims to avoid model quality questions?

References and links: Confluence (INF-serve-moat-2025), Jira (GTMP-421), GitHub PR (repo/positioning-assets/pull/17).

Drafted by: Riley Kapoor; review requested from Maya, Carlos, Priya.

Tone guidance for final copy: engineer-respecting, precise about outcomes, avoid hype about "AGI" or model magic; instead stress measurable operational gains and customer-impact stories.
